title: The preacher (Kern ch. 10)
hook: whoever keeps even one verse of this sutra is to be honored
tomorrow: The stupa in the sky (Kern ch. 11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the attendant and the son stood up and asked, and each got a promise of his own. Your line: them too. Whose name did you say out loud? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

How much of a teaching do you have to carry before you count as carrying it? The whole book? A degree? A robe and a title? A grandmother who knows one proverb and says it at exactly the right moment, every time, is she a teacher? Chapter ten of the Lotus Sutra answers that question, and its answer is smaller than the question seems to call for. The Buddha turns to a bodhisattva named Bhaishajyaraja, the Medicine King, and starts talking about a figure the chapter is named for. Not a great disciple. Not a Buddha. Just someone who passes the words along. Today: the preacher.
screen: `HOW MUCH DO YOU HAVE TO CARRY?` → `ONE PROVERB, RIGHT ON TIME.` → `THE ONE WHO PASSES IT ALONG.`

segments.voice: First, the size of it. Whoever hears even a single verse of this sutra, the Buddha says, and is glad of it even for one moment, he foretells their awakening. One verse. One moment. Then he goes further: whoever keeps it, reads it, explains it or copies it, even one verse, and honors the book with flowers and incense, is to be honored as if they were the Tathagata himself. Second, the messenger. Whoever explains this teaching to even one person, even quietly, in private, is a messenger the Tathagata has sent. The preacher in this chapter isn't defined by a crowd. One listener is enough. Third, a picture. A man in dry country needs water, so he digs. The sand comes up dry, and he keeps digging. Then the earth turns damp. Then it turns to mud. He knows water is close. Hearing this teaching, the Buddha says, is like that damp earth: a sign that awakening is near. Fourth, how to do it. The chapter gives the preacher a room, a robe and a seat. The room is compassion for all beings. The robe is patience, gentleness under pressure. The seat is seeing that all things are empty. Enter the room, put on the robe, sit on the seat, and then speak. So the chapter's preacher isn't the loudest voice. It's anyone who carries one verse, kindly, patiently, to one other person. The bar is low. The honor is high.
screen: `EVEN ONE VERSE, EVEN ONE MOMENT.` · `ONE LISTENER MAKES A MESSENGER.` · `DIGGING FOR WATER IN DRY GROUND.` · `A ROOM, A ROBE, A SEAT.` · then, large: `EVEN ONE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: honor one person who teaches. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind someone who handed you even one thing you still use. A line from a book. A way to fold a shirt. How to apologize. What to do with your hands when you're scared. It doesn't have to be a classroom teacher. See their face. Remember the moment they said it. Then, in whatever way feels natural to you, bow to them inwardly. Let the thanks be quiet and whole. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The preacher. In chapter ten, anyone who keeps or explains even one verse, even to one person, honored as a messenger of the Tathagata. Today's word.
Your line: even one verse. Today, pass along one line that once helped you, to one person, even in a text. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that treasure the Lotus Sutra, people keep, recite, copy and explain the sutra, and the one who teaches it is honored; chapter ten is where the sutra itself praises that work.

pairs: water is close; awakening is near

even one person, even in private, says the chapter.

fork.setup: you're digging for water in dry country. you've dug a while, and the sand is still dry. what do you do?
options: give up: there's no water here.
keep digging until the earth turns damp.
start a new hole somewhere else.
fork.reveal: the digger keeps going. damp earth, then mud: he knows water is near. the Buddha says hearing this teaching is that damp earth.

original.note: Sanskrit: one who recites or preaches the dharma, the 'preacher' of chapter ten.

trapdoor: what you thought: a preacher is someone with a pulpit and a crowd.
what it means: anyone who keeps, reads, copies or explains even one verse, even to one person, honored as the Tathagata's messenger.
what a scholar hears: dharmabhanaka, a reciter of the dharma, told to enter the room of compassion, wear the robe of patience and sit on the seat of emptiness.

notes: Chapter paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 10, not quoted (wording unverified). Check: one verse heard with a moment of gladness leads to a prediction; keeping, reading, explaining, copying and honoring the book with flowers and incense; such a person honored as the Tathagata.
